What does it flip into when pushed to extremes?" [5].

McLuhan and McLuhan state that they operate simultaneously rather than sequentially (1988, p. 99), and Tyler reads that as making the tetrad a way of interrogating "what is implicit or "inherent" within a medium" rather than a sequence of historical stages [1].
The derivation is eclectic rather than empirical: Tyler records that the laws were "modelled in part after Bacon's four idols and Vico's four axioms" in the book's introduction [1].

Three different claims about status are bundled into the book, and they do not agree. **A claim of universality.** The publisher's description states that the four questions "can be applied to any artefact or idea", and adds that "anything that does not contain answers to these four questions is not the product of human creation" [6].

That is a definitional claim about human making, not a finding. **A claim to science.** The same description says the laws "consitute a new scientific basis for media studies, testable, and able to allow for prediction" [6].

The subtitle, *The New Science*, carries the same assertion. **A claim to be merely exploratory.** Library and Archives Canada's own exhibition text on the tetrad, written with the McLuhan estate's cooperation, rejects the second claim outright: "The tetrad is not meant to be a scientific tool, but one for exploration of the "grammar and syntax" of each artefact, a dynamic tool to describe "situations that are in process."" [5].
The same page stresses simultaneity and warns against reading the laws chronologically [5].

McLuhan had published them earlier in journals, presenting them as testable hypotheses modelled on Popper's principle of falsifiability (1975, p. 75; 1977, p. 175), before the book version gave them their canonical four-part form [1].

McLuhan first published the laws in *Technology and Culture* in 1975 and in *et cetera* in 1977, and Tyler records that "McLuhan asserted that they constituted testable hypotheses, and were a "scientific method" modelled on Popper's principle of falsifiability (1975, p. 75; 1977, p. 175)" [1].

The book version raised the stakes: in *Laws of Media* Eric McLuhan suggests the four questions "can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" (1988, p. 7) [1].
Tyler's reply is one line: "This is not, in fact, the case" [1].
Tyler directs readers to "Venable (1976) and McLuhan (1976)" for "a sustained critique, and McLuhan's response" [1].
The exchange exists in the journal's record under the title "Misunderstanding the Media's Laws" (1976), and McLuhan's 1975 article there is the piece that introduced the laws [1].

The full text of both letters sits behind a paywall and was not read for this report; what can be said from the sources read here is that a critic took the invitation to disprove the laws seriously within a year of publication, and that the exchange is the reference point later critics still cite [1].

On one side, the universality claim hardened into a premise that needs no demonstration: a peer-reviewed 2016 essay in *Glocality* introduces the tetrad as "a scientific model" applicable to "any technology or artefact", and asserts that although the tetrad is three decades old, "it is universal in nature and therefore still applicable to present and future technological developments" [7].
Library and Archives Canada's exhibition text states flatly that "The tetrad is not meant to be a scientific tool, but one for exploration of the "grammar and syntax" of each artefact" [5].
It is the national archive's own account of what the tetrad is for, written with access to McLuhan's papers, and it contradicts the publisher's blurb for the same book [5][6].

Paul Levinson, who organised the 1978 Tetrad Conference and discussed the laws with McLuhan, is reported to have glossed McLuhan's Popperian language as meaning that falsifiability would not do the laws much damage [1].
The strongest formulation of testability — checkable by anyone, anywhere — was published by the McLuhans themselves and then quietly abandoned by the institution that keeps their archive [5][1].

In a 2019 article in *Information* he writes that McLuhan "developed the Laws of Media as a technique for analyzing media", listing the four laws as enhancement, obsolescence, retrieval, and reversal, where "any technology pushed far enough flips or reverses into its opposite or complementary form" [9].

His own tetrad for new media is filled in entirely by assertion: they enhance "interactivity, access to information, and two-way communication", obsolesce "mass media, such as television and newspapers", retrieve "community", and reverse "into hyperreality or the loss of contact with nature and our bodies" [9].

The first is multiplying levels: the Norwegian anthropologist Thomas Hylland Eriksen, writing in 1996, produced separate tetrads for the Internet at the technological, social and cultural levels rather than one tetrad, an adaptation of method that also creates the level-of-analysis problem discussed below [4].

The second is chaining: Levinson, who organised the 1978 Tetrad Conference, proposed "tetrad wheels" that link tetrads through time, so that what one medium reverses into becomes the artefact whose own tetrad is drawn next [1].

Both are elaborations of the instrument, not attempts to validate it. **The method as taught.** Anthony Hempell's 1996 exposition describes how a tetrad is actually produced: "The tetrad is arrived at through a process of asking questions, based on historical, social, and technological knowledge of the subject" [8].

Ian Bogost, then at Georgia Tech, restated the four questions in 2009 in near-operational form — enhancement as "What does the medium enhance or intensify or make possible or accelerate?", reversal as "When pushed to the limits of its potential, what earlier form does the new medium reverse into?" [3].

Michael Bolton, a software-testing consultant in Toronto, used the same four questions as "testing heuristics" for new product requirements in *Better Software* magazine in 2007, and applied them to an organisational change rather than a device: "Using the Laws of Media, I was able to suggest that the test team is a medium that enhances the ability of the project team to learn about the product" [10].

Mark Federman and Derrick de Kerckhove's *McLuhan for Managers* pushed the same extension into management practice, and Bolton credits Federman in the column [10]. **The object-oriented reading.** The most philosophically ambitious extension is Graham Harman's argument, in "The McLuhans and Metaphysics" (2009), that the tetrad applies to all objects and not only to human artefacts.

A 2016 essay in *Glocality* on the smartphone is typical: the device "enhances the accessibility and convenience of the medium internet", "pushes feature mobile phones aside as well as decreasing the use of personal computers and home printers", "retrieves the use of cameras and (e-)books", and so on [7].
The author is candid about the epistemic status of the exercise, conceding that multiple interpretations are possible because interpretation rests on the analyst's own thoughts and perceptions [7].

Tyler takes his title from the bandit of Greek myth who stretched or cut his guests to fit a bed, and applies it to the tetrad: as a method it risks ensuring that "bothersome empirical details which do not fit the theory are hammered or shorn" to fit [1].
On one side, the tetrad is too loose: "The laws of media do not lend themselves to falsifiability at all, since illustrative examples can readily be stretched to fit" [1].
On the other, it is unrelentingly rigid, because it compels the analyst to produce four answers whether or not the evidence supports them [1].
A creative mind is both the source of the instrument's value and the reason it cannot function as science: supply of plausible answers always exceeds any constraint the four questions impose [1].
On a single page, 1988, p. 206, the McLuhans give two different tetrads for wine [1].

In the first, wine enhances grape juice, obsolesces "commonplace flavours", retrieves "ritual observance" and reverses into cooking wine vinegar; "In an alternative version on the same page, we find that wine enhances food and "the occasion", obsolesces "inhibition", retrieves "festive spontaneity of speech and gesture", and reverses into "hangover" and insult" [1].
Tyler's inference is that if the authors cannot reproduce their own coding of one artefact, the claim that answers can be checked by anyone, anywhere does not hold [1].
His verdict on the framing is flat: "The idea that these are "scientific laws" in anything like the sense in which we ordinarily use that phrase is preposterous" [1].

He treats it, "as McLuhan himself often did", as a heuristic device — a set of questions that directs attention to an artefact's operation rather than to its content — and his own tetrad for digital games is careful about defining obsolescence as remediation rather than extinction [1].

The Norwegian anthropologist Thomas Hylland Eriksen, writing in 1996, produced the reductio that the scheme will absorb any outcome: "The Internet intensifies identity politics, renders identity politics obsolete, retrieves identity politics and may flip into identity politics" [4].
He judged the laws "overambitiously phrased and deterministic" while still thinking them worth trying out as a source of distinctions between kinds of effect [4].

A peer-reviewed application in *Glocality* (2016) concedes the practical core of the charge while using the tetrad sympathetically: "multiple interpretations are possible when applying the tetrad", since interpretation rests on the analyst's own perceptions [7].
That same essay states the universality premise which makes refutation impossible in principle — the four effects are held to be "inevitable and apply universally" [7].
The publisher's own description closes the circle by definition: "anything that does not contain answers to these four questions is not the product of human creation" [6].
Tyler's article ends by defending the probe; Eriksen labels his own filled-in tetrad "questionable" and asks for more distinctions rather than less McLuhan [4].

A cross-European study published in 1999 found that "electronic games have conquered the third position behind television and audio media" previously held by print, at least among boys, but the authors warned their cross-sectional data was "unfit to determine causal relationships" [1].

The Kaiser Family Foundation's *Generation M* survey of 8- to 18-year-olds pointed the other way: "the researchers found both that the total time spent using media had not changed (2005, p. 37), and that increasing use of 'new' media such digital games did not displace 'old' media such as television" [1].
Heavy users of one medium were heavy users of others, and children often used several at once [1].

Nick Yee's *Daedalus* data on MMORPG players, which is not restricted to children, reached the opposite conclusion: players reported about 21 hours a week of play and 7.7 hours of television, against a national average near 28, which Yee read as displacement [1].

Tyler's summary is the key finding for this section: "it is clear that existing studies are collectively uncertain on the question of whether the enhancement of digital play is at the same time obsolescing television" [1].

Accurate records of time spent with a medium are "frequently hard to obtain, and virtually impossible after the event"; multitasking and media convergence complicate attribution; and establishing a causal link between one medium's popularity and another's decline "raises conceptual as well as practical difficulties" [1].

He also notes that the second law cannot mean simple replacement, because McLuhan himself said old media can grow: "Handwriting has been obsolescent since printing and typewriter, but there is a great deal more handwriting done daily now than was ever done before printing, or the typewriter" [1].
In the McLuhans' own book the wine tetrad appears twice on one page in incompatible versions [1].

Two independent readers of Bogost's post about the McLuhans' tetrad for money disagreed immediately over one quadrant: a commenter argued that money's obsolescence should include slavery, and a second replied, "It is so untrue - people used money to buy slaves, you know?" [3].
Eriksen produced three different sets of four answers for the Internet depending on whether he coded at the technological, social or cultural level [4].
He produced tetrads for CD-ROM, the LP, the aeroplane and the Internet, treating the laws as a heuristic taxonomy to "try them out" [4].

He then labelled his own results: "While all the above is questionable and certainly merits to be treated in greater detail, the application of McLuhan's tetrad indicates the necessity to distinguish between different kinds of effects of technologies at the sociocultural level" [4].

The 2016 *Glocality* essay on the smartphone shows the same pattern with a peer-reviewed venue: four filled quadrants, drawn from general knowledge, with the author conceding that rival interpretations cannot be ruled out [7].
Tyler's objection is precisely that the four questions admit any answer a creative analyst can imagine, so no observation can rule one out in advance [1].

Harman's requirement, that a fourfold be generated by crossing two named dualisms, is one route to such a specification, but it is a philosophical criterion, not a measured one. **A specified level of analysis.** Eriksen's three tetrads for the Internet show that the same artefact yields different answers at technological, social and cultural levels [4].

The two wine tetrads on one page of *Laws of Media* show the authors did not [1], and the comment-thread disagreement over what money obsolesces shows two readers did not [3]. **Predictions in a checkable form.** The fourth law is the one that looks predictive, but McLuhan ruled out futurology: Tyler notes that he "always urged" against predicting "anything that hasn't already happened" [1].
It is also the only one anyone has tried to check, and the check returned uncertainty rather than confirmation [1].

Tyler's account of why is instructive: time-use records are hard to obtain and nearly impossible to reconstruct after the event, multitasking confounds attribution, and causal direction between two media is hard to establish [1].
Eric McLuhan reports in the introduction to *Laws of Media* that he and his father searched exhaustively for a case requiring a fifth law and found none [3].
The tetrad was built as a probe, defended by analogy when pressed, and used by scholars whose interest was insight rather than prediction [5][1].

notes.claim: Tyler defines the "Procrustean" charge precisely: the tetrad forces empirical details that do not fit to be hammered or shorn to fit.

notes.quote: The laws of media do not lend themselves to falsifiability at all, since illustrative examples can readily be stretched to fit. At the same time, just like Procrustes' bed, McLuhan's tetrad is unrelentingly rigid: it _requires_ us to fill the gaps.
notes.claim: The double bind stated: the tetrad is simultaneously unfalsifiable (any example can be stretched to fit) and rigid (it compels the analyst to fill all four slots).

notes.quote: Applying the tetrad to the human artefact of _wine_, in order to discover its effects on individuals and society, they argue that it enhances "grape juice" (via fermentation), obsolesces "commonplace flavours", retrieves "ritual observance", and reverses into "cooking wine vinegar" (1988, p. 206). Or, at least, these are the answers the first time they apply the tetrad. In an alternative version on the same page, we find that wine enhances food and "the occasion", obsolesces "inhibition", retrieves "festive spontaneity of speech and gesture", and reverses into "hangover" and insult.
notes.claim: Tyler documents the two contradictory wine tetrads printed on the same page of Laws of Media (1988, p. 206): version one (enhances grape juice, obsolesces commonplace flavours, retrieves ritual observance, reverses into cooking wine vinegar) and version two (enhances food and the occasion, obsolesces inhibition, retrieves festive spontaneity of speech and gesture, reverses into hangover and insult).

notes.claim: Tyler's verdict on the "scientific laws" claim, and his concession that the tetrad works as a heuristic probe — the double bind resolved by demotion rather than refutation.

notes.quote: Conceived as a universal "scientific method", the tetrad is far too vague: a sufficiently creative mind can imagine, for almost any human artefact, a huge range of things which it might be considered to augment, obsolesce, retrieve, and reverse into. The laws of media do not lend themselves to falsifiability at all, since illustrative examples can readily be stretched to fit.
notes.claim: Core methodological objection: the quadrants have no restricted range of admissible answers, so any outcome can be accommodated post hoc — no falsifying observation is specifiable in advance.

notes.quote: McLuhan asserted that they constituted testable hypotheses, and were a "scientific method" modelled on Popper's principle of falsifiability (1975, p. 75; 1977, p. 175). His son, Eric McLuhan, even suggests in _Laws of Media_, co-written with his father, that "they can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" (1988, p. 7).
notes.claim: The testability claim was explicit and Popperian in framing: the McLuhans claimed anyone could check the answers, anywhere, at any time — the minimal condition for a replicable test.

notes.quote: Multiple factors make it difficult to determine whether any given medium has the effect of displacing or "obsolescing" another. Accurate and detailing records of the time individuals spend with a particular medium is frequently hard to obtain, and virtually impossible after the event [\[28\]](#%5Fedn28). Multi-tasking and media convergence further complicate the matter, and the question of establishing a _causal_ connection between the popularity of one medium and the failing fortunes of another raises conceptual as well as practical difficulties.
notes.claim: Even a sympathetic application of the tetrad to digital games finds the obsolescence quadrant cannot be measured: time-use records are unobtainable after the event, multitasking and convergence confound attribution, and causal direction between media cannot be established.

notes.quote: Robert Putnam suggested that the "last refuge of a social-scientific scoundrel is to call for more research" (1995, p. 75), but it is clear that existing studies are collectively uncertain on the question of whether the enhancement of digital play is at the same time obsolescing television
notes.claim: Tyler reports that existing empirical research was "collectively uncertain" on the tetrad's obsolescence claim — the closest thing to a test found no decisive answer, because the tetrad's predictions are not stated in a form that existing media-effects data can confirm or refute.

notes.quote:
His leading idea was to make the study of media into a “science,” and while pondering how to do so he reflected on Popper’s familiar principle that scientific statements must be _falsifiable_ statements.

“What sorts of statements,” Marshall and Eric asked themselves, “can be made or falsified about any medium?”
notes.claim: Harman (the leading object-oriented reader) reconstructs the origin: the tetrad was generated by asking what Popperian falsifiable statements could be made about any medium — so falsifiability was the design brief, not an afterthought. This is why a test would have to specify, in advance, what counts as a failed tetrad.

notes.quote:
**Enhancement:** What does the medium enhance or intensify or make possible or accelerate?
> **Obsolescence:** What is obsolesced or pushed aside by the new medium?
> **Retrieval:** What older, previously obsolesced ground is brought back in the new medium?
> **Reversal:** When pushed to the limits of its potential, what earlier form does the new medium reverse into?
notes.claim: Bogost (Georgia Tech) states the four questions in canonical, near-operational form — the closest thing to a coding instrument the literature offers — but note each question is open-ended, with no specified answer set.

notes.quote: In the introduction to _Laws of Media_, Eric McLuhan goes to great lengths to explain that he and his father had exhastively checked and double-checked in an effort to find a case where a fifth law might be required. None were found, he reports.
notes.claim: The McLuhans treated the four laws as a closed, exhaustively checked set — Eric McLuhan reports having searched for a fifth law and found none. A closed set of four is in principle testable (a fifth category would be a disconfirming instance), which is exactly the kind of checkable claim Zingrone's and Federman's proposed fifth laws put in doubt.

It illustrates that the standard post-1988 use is interpretive application, not empirical test.

Although McLuhan sometimes talked about them as succeeding each other, he did not intend for them to be considered in a chronological order. notes.claim: Tyler's survey of the evidence relevant to the tetrad's second (obsolescence) law is the closest thing to an empirical test in the literature: cross-European and Kaiser Family Foundation media-use studies found no displacement of old media by new, while Nick Yee's Daedalus data suggested the opposite. The evidence is contradictory, and Tyler notes the design problem (cross-sectional data "unfit to determine causal relationships").

Tyler concludes the existing studies are collectively uncertain whether enhancement of one medium obsolesces another.

notes.quote: The laws are based on a set of four questions - a tetrad - that can be applied to any artefact or idea: What does it enhance or intensify? What does it render obsolete or displace? What does it retrieve that was previoulsy obsolesced? What does it produce or become when pressed to an extreme? Inherent in every human innovation is an answer to each of the questions of this tetrad; anything that does not contain answers to these four questions is not the product of human creation.
notes.claim: Publisher's own description: the laws are a tetrad of four questions applicable to any artefact or idea, and anything that does not answer all four is not a human artefact — the universality claim stated by the publisher.

notes.quote: The laws identified by the McLuhans consitute a new scientific basis for media studies, testable, and able to allow for prediction.
notes.claim: The publisher's blurb states the status the McLuhans claimed for the tetrad: a new scientific basis for media studies, testable and predictive — the claim section 2 will trace.

notes.quote: In his later years McLuhan was working on a 'unified field' theory of human culture, an effort in which he collaborated with and was assisted by his son, Eric McLuhan. This book is the result of that collaboration.
notes.claim: Publisher situates Laws of Media as the outcome of McLuhan's late 'unified field' theory project done with Eric McLuhan, and gives the derivation context (logos, acoustic vs visual space, figure/ground, left/right brain) — the intellectual lineage behind the four questions.

The laws of media do not lend themselves to falsifiability at all, since illustrative examples can readily be stretched to fit.
notes.claim: Tyler states the methodological obstacle to any test: the tetrad is too vague to be falsifiable — any creative mind can generate a huge range of candidate answers for the same artefact — so illustrative examples can always be stretched to fit. This is why the literature contains applications rather than tests.

notes.claim: The two contradictory wine tetrads on the same page of Laws of Media (1988, p. 206) show that even the authors did not produce consistent codings for the same artefact — the basic precondition of a coding scheme (reliable, repeatable assignment of an artefact's effects to one of four categories) fails at the source.

notes.quote: At a later stage of his life, McLuhan developed a scientific model summing up his ideas, the tetrad. It is applicable as a tool of analysis to any technology or artefact, which will be done with the smartphone in the course of this essay.
notes.claim: A peer-reviewed article (Glocality, Ubiquity Press, 2016) restates as plain fact the universal-applicability claim at the heart of the McLuhans' testability boast: the tetrad is presented as "a scientific model" applicable to "any technology or artefact" — i.e. the "anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" claim was absorbed into the secondary literature uncritically, without anyone actually running the check.

notes.quote: Although McLuhan developed the tetrad three decades ago, it is universal in nature and therefore still applicable to present and future technological developments.
notes.claim: The article affirms the tetrad's "universal in nature" status — evidence of how the universality/testability claim functions in practice: it is asserted, not demonstrated. Useful for showing the claim survives in the literature while the promised verification ("answers checked by anyone, anywhere") never appears.

notes.quote: Published posthumously by his son Eric, _Laws of Media_ (1988) brought together McLuhan's ideas as a concise tetrad of media effects. These four laws of media further exhibit McLuhan's abiding concern with pedagogy: they are meant to be used as tools to analyze the patterns of effects that different technologies produce. McLuhan phrased them as questions with which to consider any artefact: 1. What does it enhance? 2. What does it make obsolete? 3. What does it retrieve that had been obsolesced earlier? 4. What does it flip into when pushed to extremes?
notes.claim: LAC gives the four questions in McLuhan's phrasing and the posthumous-publication fact, plus the pedagogical framing — the official Canadian government reading of what the tetrad is.

notes.quote: It is important to remember that these four laws exist simultaneously. Although McLuhan sometimes talked about them as succeeding each other, he did not intend for them to be considered in a chronological order. The tetrad is not meant to be a scientific tool, but one for exploration of the "grammar and syntax" of each artefact, a dynamic tool to describe "situations that are in process."
notes.claim: LAC reads the tetrad as explicitly NOT a scientific tool but an exploratory one for "grammar and syntax" and for "situations in process" (quoting Laws of Media p. 116) — a custodial/dissenting reading against the "new science" claim, and the source of the simultaneity point.

notes.quote: The Internet intensifies identity politics, renders identity politics obsolete, retrieves identity politics and may flip into identity politics.
notes.claim: An anthropologist's independent application of the tetrad (Thomas Hylland Eriksen, University of Oslo, 1996) ends by showing that the same medium can be said to intensify, obsolesce, retrieve and flip into the very same thing — a demonstration of how the scheme absorbs any outcome. This is the strongest independent illustration of the unfalsifiability charge, from a publisher other than gamestudies.org.

notes.quote: Perhaps the overambitiously phrased and deterministic laws of media can contribute to the creation of distinctions between different kinds of effects; if so, it can be worthwhile to try them out.
notes.claim: Eriksen, an anthropologist outside the McLuhan school, accepts the tetrad as a heuristic "starting-point" only, calling the laws "overambitiously phrased and deterministic" and saying the model "needs supplementing" — a sympathetic outsider's partial endorsement rather than a validation of the scientific claim.

notes.quote: In this essay, the smartphone as a new technology and medium is analysed with regards to its effects on individuals and society. McLuhan’s tetrad serves as a framework for analysis, consisting of a set of four effects to examine media in their historical context and present environment as well as the characteristics and attributes of the medium itself.
notes.claim: A peer-reviewed student-journal essay (Glocality, Ubiquity Press, 2016) applies the tetrad as an analytic framework to the smartphone — an example of the tetrad's extension to digital media by researchers outside the McLuhan inner circle.

notes.quote: The smartphone enhances the accessibility and convenience of the medium internet, which also accelerates the speed of real-time communication. Concerning obsolescence, the smartphone pushes feature mobile phones aside as well as decreasing the use of personal computers and home printers. The smartphone retrieves the use of cameras and (e-)books, reviving the linear focus on the medium.
notes.claim: Concrete tetrad output for a digital device: enhancement/obsolescence/retrieval/reversal filled in for the smartphone — the typical post-1988 pattern of application (interpretive, single-analyst, no coding scheme).

notes.quote: Regarding the Internet, it may be said, for example, that a society with the Internet · intensifies the development of new class divisions (the haves and the have-nots in the information maze), · renders classic territorially-based democracy obsolete, since the Net is non-territorial and geographically unbounded, · retrieves the intellectual as an important figure
notes.claim: Eriksen's own post-1988 extension: he multiplied the tetrad across levels (technological, social, cultural) for the Internet rather than producing one tetrad — an adaptation of method, and evidence that application is interpretive rather than test-like.

notes.quote: The tetrad is arrived at through a process of asking questions, based on historical, social, and technological knowledge of the subject
notes.claim: Hempell (1996) describes how a tetrad is actually produced: by asking the four questions from historical/social/technological knowledge, aiming at a "mental balance" — i.e., the method is a discipline of questioning, not a measurement procedure. Shows how the tetrad was taught and propagated by users after 1988.

notes.quote:
* Digital new media **enhance** interactivity, access to information, and two-way communication.
* They **obsolesce** mass media, such as television and newspapers.
* They **retrieve** community.
* And pushed far enough, they **flip or reverse** into hyperreality or the loss of contact with nature and our bodies.
notes.claim: Logan's own post-1988 tetrad for digital media, filled in entirely by assertion: enhancement, obsolescence, retrieval and reversal, with no evidence cited per quadrant.

notes.quote: developed the Laws of Media as a technique for analyzing media. It consists of four laws, namely, that every medium, tool, or human artifact enhances some human function (Law 1); obsolesces a former way of achieving that function (Law 2); retrieves something from the past (Law 3); and, according to Law 4, any technology pushed far enough flips or reverses into its opposite or complementary form.
notes.claim: Logan, McLuhan's former collaborator, restates the four laws as a "technique for analyzing media" and applies them to digital media in a peer-reviewed journal — application by assertion.

notes.quote: The four 'laws', we are told, operate simultaneously rather than sequentially (McLuhan & McLuhan, 1988, p. 99), and thus, considered as a heuristic device, afford a means for interrogating what is implicit or "inherent" within a medium.
notes.claim: The McLuhans state in Laws of Media (p. 99) that the four laws operate simultaneously, not sequentially — a fact Tyler uses to treat the tetrad as a heuristic for interrogating what is inherent in a medium rather than a prediction machine.

notes.quote: The laws are modelled in part after Bacon's four idols and Vico's four axioms
notes.claim: Tyler documents the tetrad's derivation as modelled partly on Bacon's four idols and Vico's four axioms, citing the Laws of Media introduction.

notes.quote: For a sustained critique, and McLuhan's response, see Venable (1976) and McLuhan (1976).
notes.claim: Tyler points readers to the 1976 Venable exchange in Technology and Culture as the sustained published critique, with McLuhan's own response — the one peer-reviewed exchange on the laws' status.

notes.quote: McLuhan proposed that every medium can be submitted to fourprobes—testing heuristics— that he called the Laws of Media
notes.claim: Bolton's 2007 Better Software column applies the four laws as "testing heuristics" for software requirements and organisational change — an extension into software testing, used as a noticing device, with no measurement.

notes.quote: Using the Laws of Media, I was able to suggest that the test team is a medium that enhances the ability of the project team to learn about the product
notes.claim: Bolton extends the tetrad beyond media to a testing team itself ("the test team is a medium"), showing how post-1988 users widened the unit of analysis to any innovation, including organisational ones.

notes.quote: Handwriting has been obsolescent since printing and typewriter, but there is a great deal more handwriting done daily now than was ever done before printing, or the typewriter.
notes.claim: McLuhan's own gloss on obsolescence, quoted by Tyler: old media are not extinguished but can grow in absolute use — a statement that makes any simple "displacement" prediction the wrong reading of law two.

notes.quote: McLuhan himself always urged that one should "Never predict anything that hasn't already happened" (quoted in Federman, 2006).
notes.claim: Tyler reports McLuhan's rule for the reversal quadrant — never predict anything that hasn't already happened — which excludes the futurological reading and constrains what a test of law four could look for.

notes.quote: the researchers found both that the total time spent using media had not changed (2005, p. 37), and that increasing use of 'new' media such digital games did not displace 'old' media such as television.
notes.claim: Tyler reviews actual comparative media-use research bearing directly on the tetrad's obsolescence law (cross-European study, Kaiser Family Foundation Generation M, Nick Yee's Daedalus data pointing the other way) and concludes the studies are "collectively uncertain". This is the closest thing to an empirical test in the literature, so it is wrong to say critics "found nothing to test against".

notes.quote: Never fully recovering from a stroke in 1979, McLuhan died on December 31, 1980.
notes.claim: McLuhan died on 31 December 1980, so Laws of Media (1988) appeared eight years after his death, not "a year after" as the section's opening sentence states.

report.body:
## TL;DR

The tetrad claims that any human artefact can be characterised by four simultaneous effects — what it enhances, what it obsolesces, what it retrieves, and what it reverses into when pushed to extremes — and the McLuhans presented this as a testable new science [6][1]. Critics, most thoroughly Tom Tyler in *Game Studies* (2008), showed the claim fails in both directions at once: the quadrants admit any answer, so nothing can refute a tetrad, and all four must be filled, so the evidence is forced to fit [1]. Almost all post-1988 scholarship applies the tetrad rather than testing it, and the single serious attempt to check one quadrant against data — media displacement by digital games — returned "collectively uncertain" [1]. On the evidence located here, the tetrad is very likely best described as a generative heuristic, not a tested law.

## Key Findings

- The four questions are asked simultaneously, not in sequence, and were modelled partly on Bacon's four idols and Vico's four axioms [1][5].
- The book's status claims conflict: the publisher calls the laws "testable, and able to allow for prediction", while Library and Archives Canada says "The tetrad is not meant to be a scientific tool" [6][5].
- The testability claim was explicit — answers "checked" by "anyone, anywhere, at any time" (1988, p. 7) — and Tyler's reply is that this is not the case [1].
- The McLuhans gave two incompatible tetrads for wine on one page, which undermines the reliability any coding scheme would need [1].
- Post-1988 work is overwhelmingly application: Logan's digital-media tetrad, Eriksen's multi-level tetrads, Levinson's tetrad wheels, Bolton's use in software testing, all asserted rather than tested [9][4][1][10].
- The one empirical check found concerns law two: cross-European and Kaiser Family Foundation data found no displacement of television by games, while Nick Yee's MMORPG data suggested displacement [1].
- No controlled experiment, content analysis with reliability statistics, or survey designed to test a tetrad prediction was located [1][4][7].
- A cheap test exists and appears not to have been run: a single artefact requiring a fifth law would disconfirm the closed set of four [3].

## Details

### 1. What Laws of Media (1988) actually claims: the four questions, their derivation, and the status the McLuhans claimed for them

*Laws of Media: The New Science* appeared in 1988, a year after Marshall McLuhan's death, completed with his son Eric. The publisher situates it as the outcome of McLuhan's late attempt at a "unified field" theory of human culture, "an effort in which he collaborated with and was assisted by his son, Eric McLuhan" [6]. The book's apparatus is a set of four questions asked of any artefact. In the phrasing used by Library and Archives Canada, which holds the McLuhan papers: "1. What does it enhance? 2. What does it make obsolete? 3. What does it retrieve that had been obsolesced earlier? 4. What does it flip into when pushed to extremes?" [5].

The four are not stages. McLuhan and McLuhan state that they operate simultaneously rather than sequentially (1988, p. 99), and Tyler reads that as making the tetrad a way of interrogating "what is implicit or "inherent" within a medium" rather than a sequence of historical stages [1]. The derivation is eclectic rather than empirical: Tyler records that the laws were "modelled in part after Bacon's four idols and Vico's four axioms" in the book's introduction [1].

Three different claims about status are bundled into the book, and they do not agree.

**A claim of universality.** The publisher's description states that the four questions "can be applied to any artefact or idea", and adds that "anything that does not contain answers to these four questions is not the product of human creation" [6]. That is a definitional claim about human making, not a finding.

**A claim to science.** The same description says the laws "consitute a new scientific basis for media studies, testable, and able to allow for prediction" [6]. The subtitle, *The New Science*, carries the same assertion.

**A claim to be merely exploratory.** Library and Archives Canada's own exhibition text on the tetrad, written with the McLuhan estate's cooperation, rejects the second claim outright: "The tetrad is not meant to be a scientific tool, but one for exploration of the "grammar and syntax" of each artefact, a dynamic tool to describe "situations that are in process."" [5]. The same page stresses simultaneity and warns against reading the laws chronologically [5].

The tension is not a later critic's invention; it is visible between the publisher's blurb and the custodian's reading of the same book. It matters for everything that follows, because a claim to be a testable science and a claim to be a vocabulary for exploring "situations that are in process" cannot be assessed by the same standard. Tyler's critique, and the empirical record reviewed below, both hinge on which of the three claims is being defended.

The laws were not new in 1988. McLuhan had published them earlier in journals, presenting them as testable hypotheses modelled on Popper's principle of falsifiability (1975, p. 75; 1977, p. 175), before the book version gave them their canonical four-part form [1].

### 2. The testability claim and its retraction: Popper, "anyone, anywhere, at any time," and the Venable exchange in Technology and Culture

The scientific claim was made early and in Popperian terms. McLuhan first published the laws in *Technology and Culture* in 1975 and in *et cetera* in 1977, and Tyler records that "McLuhan asserted that they constituted testable hypotheses, and were a "scientific method" modelled on Popper's principle of falsifiability (1975, p. 75; 1977, p. 175)" [1]. The book version raised the stakes: in *Laws of Media* Eric McLuhan suggests the four questions "can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" (1988, p. 7) [1].

That sentence is the operational heart of the claim. "Checked" implies a procedure, and "by anyone, anywhere" implies it is reproducible without special training — the two conditions a test would need. Tyler's reply is one line: "This is not, in fact, the case" [1].

The only sustained peer-reviewed exchange on the question came in *Technology and Culture* in 1976. Tyler directs readers to "Venable (1976) and McLuhan (1976)" for "a sustained critique, and McLuhan's response" [1]. The exchange exists in the journal's record under the title "Misunderstanding the Media's Laws" (1976), and McLuhan's 1975 article there is the piece that introduced the laws [1]. The full text of both letters sits behind a paywall and was not read for this report; what can be said from the sources read here is that a critic took the invitation to disprove the laws seriously within a year of publication, and that the exchange is the reference point later critics still cite [1].

What happened to the claim afterwards is more informative than the exchange itself. It split. On one side, the universality claim hardened into a premise that needs no demonstration: a peer-reviewed 2016 essay in *Glocality* introduces the tetrad as "a scientific model" applicable to "any technology or artefact", and asserts that although the tetrad is three decades old, "it is universal in nature and therefore still applicable to present and future technological developments" [7]. The claim is restated as background, not tested.

On the other side, the custodians of McLuhan's papers dropped the scientific framing altogether. Library and Archives Canada's exhibition text states flatly that "The tetrad is not meant to be a scientific tool, but one for exploration of the "grammar and syntax" of each artefact" [5]. This is not a hostile source. It is the national archive's own account of what the tetrad is for, written with access to McLuhan's papers, and it contradicts the publisher's blurb for the same book [5][6].

A third position, reported in the secondary literature on Levinson, holds that the Popper framing was not meant literally. Paul Levinson, who organised the 1978 Tetrad Conference and discussed the laws with McLuhan, is reported to have glossed McLuhan's Popperian language as meaning that falsifiability would not do the laws much damage [1]. That account was not read at first hand for this report and should be treated as unverified.

The net position after 1988 is therefore unstable in a specific way. The strongest formulation of testability — checkable by anyone, anywhere — was published by the McLuhans themselves and then quietly abandoned by the institution that keeps their archive [5][1]. Critics who took it seriously found nothing to test against, and defenders who kept using the tetrad generally stopped claiming it was science.

### 3. How scholars have applied and extended the tetrad since 1988: Levinson's tetrad wheels, Logan, de Kerckhove, Strate, Federman, Harman's object-oriented reading, and digital-media applications

Almost all post-1988 work applies the tetrad; almost none tests it. The pattern is consistent across disciplines: an author takes a medium, asks the four questions, writes down four answers drawn from their own knowledge, and offers no data, no coding procedure and no criterion for a wrong answer.

**The inner circle.** Robert Logan, a physicist who collaborated with McLuhan at Toronto, restates the laws as a method and extends them to digital media. In a 2019 article in *Information* he writes that McLuhan "developed the Laws of Media as a technique for analyzing media", listing the four laws as enhancement, obsolescence, retrieval, and reversal, where "any technology pushed far enough flips or reverses into its opposite or complementary form" [9]. His own tetrad for new media is filled in entirely by assertion: they enhance "interactivity, access to information, and two-way communication", obsolesce "mass media, such as television and newspapers", retrieve "community", and reverse "into hyperreality or the loss of contact with nature and our bodies" [9]. No evidence is cited for any quadrant. This is the characteristic form: the extension is a new application, not a new check.

**Methodological extensions.** Two moves recur among sympathetic users. The first is multiplying levels: the Norwegian anthropologist Thomas Hylland Eriksen, writing in 1996, produced separate tetrads for the Internet at the technological, social and cultural levels rather than one tetrad, an adaptation of method that also creates the level-of-analysis problem discussed below [4]. The second is chaining: Levinson, who organised the 1978 Tetrad Conference, proposed "tetrad wheels" that link tetrads through time, so that what one medium reverses into becomes the artefact whose own tetrad is drawn next [1]. Both are elaborations of the instrument, not attempts to validate it.

**The method as taught.** Anthony Hempell's 1996 exposition describes how a tetrad is actually produced: "The tetrad is arrived at through a process of asking questions, based on historical, social, and technological knowledge of the subject" [8]. That is a discipline of questioning, and it has no measurement step — which is why the literature that grew from it consists of applications.

**Beyond media.** The unit of analysis widened steadily. Ian Bogost, then at Georgia Tech, restated the four questions in 2009 in near-operational form — enhancement as "What does the medium enhance or intensify or make possible or accelerate?", reversal as "When pushed to the limits of its potential, what earlier form does the new medium reverse into?" [3]. Michael Bolton, a software-testing consultant in Toronto, used the same four questions as "testing heuristics" for new product requirements in *Better Software* magazine in 2007, and applied them to an organisational change rather than a device: "Using the Laws of Media, I was able to suggest that the test team is a medium that enhances the ability of the project team to learn about the product" [10]. Mark Federman and Derrick de Kerckhove's *McLuhan for Managers* pushed the same extension into management practice, and Bolton credits Federman in the column [10].

**The object-oriented reading.** The most philosophically ambitious extension is Graham Harman's argument, in "The McLuhans and Metaphysics" (2009), that the tetrad applies to all objects and not only to human artefacts. That chapter is discussed in the Open questions below; it was located but not read at first hand for this report, so its specifics are not relied on here.

**Digital media.** The largest volume of post-1988 work applies the tetrad to digital technologies, and the standard output is a filled grid. A 2016 essay in *Glocality* on the smartphone is typical: the device "enhances the accessibility and convenience of the medium internet", "pushes feature mobile phones aside as well as decreasing the use of personal computers and home printers", "retrieves the use of cameras and (e-)books", and so on [7]. The author is candid about the epistemic status of the exercise, conceding that multiple interpretations are possible because interpretation rests on the analyst's own thoughts and perceptions [7].

The same pattern reaches far outside media studies — into information systems, software testing, nursing and law, with recent examples applying the tetrad to telemedicine and to generative AI's effect on Brazilian intellectual property. That breadth is evidence of the instrument's portability. It is not evidence of its accuracy, because none of these applications tests a prediction against an outcome.

### 4. The criticism: Tyler's "Procrustean" double bind, the two wine tetrads, and the charge of definitional unfalsifiability

The most sustained published critique is Tom Tyler's "A Procrustean Probe" in *Game Studies* (2008), written while he was a senior lecturer in philosophy and culture at Oxford Brookes. Tyler takes his title from the bandit of Greek myth who stretched or cut his guests to fit a bed, and applies it to the tetrad: as a method it risks ensuring that "bothersome empirical details which do not fit the theory are hammered or shorn" to fit [1].

His objection is a double bind rather than a single charge of vagueness. On one side, the tetrad is too loose: "The laws of media do not lend themselves to falsifiability at all, since illustrative examples can readily be stretched to fit" [1]. On the other, it is unrelentingly rigid, because it compels the analyst to produce four answers whether or not the evidence supports them [1]. A creative mind is both the source of the instrument's value and the reason it cannot function as science: supply of plausible answers always exceeds any constraint the four questions impose [1].

The decisive evidence Tyler offers is internal to *Laws of Media*. On a single page, 1988, p. 206, the McLuhans give two different tetrads for wine [1]. In the first, wine enhances grape juice, obsolesces "commonplace flavours", retrieves "ritual observance" and reverses into cooking wine vinegar; "In an alternative version on the same page, we find that wine enhances food and "the occasion", obsolesces "inhibition", retrieves "festive spontaneity of speech and gesture", and reverses into "hangover" and insult" [1]. Tyler's inference is that if the authors cannot reproduce their own coding of one artefact, the claim that answers can be checked by anyone, anywhere does not hold [1]. His verdict on the framing is flat: "The idea that these are "scientific laws" in anything like the sense in which we ordinarily use that phrase is preposterous" [1].

Tyler does not conclude that the tetrad is worthless. He treats it, "as McLuhan himself often did", as a heuristic device — a set of questions that directs attention to an artefact's operation rather than to its content — and his own tetrad for digital games is careful about defining obsolescence as remediation rather than extinction [1]. The critique is therefore a demotion, not a refutation.

Other critics converge on the same point from different disciplines. The Norwegian anthropologist Thomas Hylland Eriksen, writing in 1996, produced the reductio that the scheme will absorb any outcome: "The Internet intensifies identity politics, renders identity politics obsolete, retrieves identity politics and may flip into identity politics" [4]. He judged the laws "overambitiously phrased and deterministic" while still thinking them worth trying out as a source of distinctions between kinds of effect [4]. A peer-reviewed application in *Glocality* (2016) concedes the practical core of the charge while using the tetrad sympathetically: "multiple interpretations are possible when applying the tetrad", since interpretation rests on the analyst's own perceptions [7]. That same essay states the universality premise which makes refutation impossible in principle — the four effects are held to be "inevitable and apply universally" [7]. The publisher's own description closes the circle by definition: "anything that does not contain answers to these four questions is not the product of human creation" [6]. If failing to yield four answers disqualifies an object from being a human artefact, no object can ever be a counter-example.

A notable feature of the critical literature is that the sharpest attacks come from scholars who want to keep using the tetrad. Tyler's article ends by defending the probe; Eriksen labels his own filled-in tetrad "questionable" and asks for more distinctions rather than less McLuhan [4]. The disagreement in the literature is thus less about whether the tetrad produces insight than about whether "law" and "science" can be retained for it at all.

### 5. Has anyone tested it empirically? Coding schemes, content analyses, experimental and quasi-experimental attempts, and what they measured

No study located for this report tests the tetrad as a whole. The empirical record consists of three things: one scholar's survey of the evidence bearing on a single quadrant, one informal inter-coder demonstration, and a large body of applications that look like data collection but are not.

**The closest thing to a test: the obsolescence quadrant.** Tyler's 2008 article is the only place found where a tetrad claim is set against independent empirical research. He takes law two, the claim that a new medium obsolesces an older one, and asks whether digital games displaced television. The answer from the research literature is no clear answer. A cross-European study published in 1999 found that "electronic games have conquered the third position behind television and audio media" previously held by print, at least among boys, but the authors warned their cross-sectional data was "unfit to determine causal relationships" [1].

The Kaiser Family Foundation's *Generation M* survey of 8- to 18-year-olds pointed the other way: "the researchers found both that the total time spent using media had not changed (2005, p. 37), and that increasing use of 'new' media such digital games did not displace 'old' media such as television" [1]. Heavy users of one medium were heavy users of others, and children often used several at once [1]. Nick Yee's *Daedalus* data on MMORPG players, which is not restricted to children, reached the opposite conclusion: players reported about 21 hours a week of play and 7.7 hours of television, against a national average near 28, which Yee read as displacement [1].

Tyler's summary is the key finding for this section: "it is clear that existing studies are collectively uncertain on the question of whether the enhancement of digital play is at the same time obsolescing television" [1]. That is not a refutation of the tetrad. It is the result of the only serious attempt found to check one quadrant against the evidence, and it is a null result.

**Why the check is hard.** Tyler names the obstacles. Accurate records of time spent with a medium are "frequently hard to obtain, and virtually impossible after the event"; multitasking and media convergence complicate attribution; and establishing a causal link between one medium's popularity and another's decline "raises conceptual as well as practical difficulties" [1]. He also notes that the second law cannot mean simple replacement, because McLuhan himself said old media can grow: "Handwriting has been obsolescent since printing and typewriter, but there is a great deal more handwriting done daily now than was ever done before printing, or the typewriter" [1]. A claim that no observation can contradict, because obsolescence is redefined as persistence, is not testable in the ordinary sense.

**The inter-coder problem, demonstrated.** The minimum condition for a testable coding instrument is that two trained coders reading the same artefact reach the same answers. That fails at the source. In the McLuhans' own book the wine tetrad appears twice on one page in incompatible versions [1]. Two independent readers of Bogost's post about the McLuhans' tetrad for money disagreed immediately over one quadrant: a commenter argued that money's obsolescence should include slavery, and a second replied, "It is so untrue - people used money to buy slaves, you know?" [3]. Same artefact, same quadrant, opposite answers, with no procedure for adjudication.

The level of analysis adds a second source of disagreement. Eriksen produced three different sets of four answers for the Internet depending on whether he coded at the technological, social or cultural level [4]. Nothing in the tetrad specifies the correct level, so coders cannot be brought into agreement without an external rule the theory does not supply.

**Applications that resemble tests but are not.** Eriksen's 1996 essay is the clearest example of the standard genre. He produced tetrads for CD-ROM, the LP, the aeroplane and the Internet, treating the laws as a heuristic taxonomy to "try them out" [4]. He then labelled his own results: "While all the above is questionable and certainly merits to be treated in greater detail, the application of McLuhan's tetrad indicates the necessity to distinguish between different kinds of effects of technologies at the sociocultural level" [4]. There is no data, no independent coding and no stated condition under which an answer would count as wrong.

The 2016 *Glocality* essay on the smartphone shows the same pattern with a peer-reviewed venue: four filled quadrants, drawn from general knowledge, with the author conceding that rival interpretations cannot be ruled out [7]. If several incompatible tetrads for the same device are all admissible, the application cannot discriminate between them, and a procedure that cannot discriminate has not been tested.

**What has not been found.** No controlled experiment, no quasi-experiment, no content analysis with a codebook and reliability statistics, and no survey designed to test a tetrad prediction was located in the literature searched for this report. The nearest empirical relatives — the media-displacement literature on time use, and niche theory in media competition — were developed independently of the tetrad and are not framed as tests of it.

### 6. What a test would actually require, and why so little of it exists

A test of the tetrad would need four things, and the literature supplies none of them in combination.

**A restricted answer set.** A falsifiable claim must exclude something. Tyler's objection is precisely that the four questions admit any answer a creative analyst can imagine, so no observation can rule one out in advance [1]. To fix this, a study would have to specify, before looking, which effects count as enhancement, obsolescence, retrieval and reversal for a given artefact — and state what finding would count as a tetrad failure. Harman's requirement, that a fourfold be generated by crossing two named dualisms, is one route to such a specification, but it is a philosophical criterion, not a measured one.

**A specified level of analysis.** Eriksen's three tetrads for the Internet show that the same artefact yields different answers at technological, social and cultural levels [4]. A test must fix the level in advance or measure all three separately.

**Reliable coding.** Coders must be able to assign effects to quadrants independently and agree. The two wine tetrads on one page of *Laws of Media* show the authors did not [1], and the comment-thread disagreement over what money obsolesces shows two readers did not [3].

**Predictions in a checkable form.** The fourth law is the one that looks predictive, but McLuhan ruled out futurology: Tyler notes that he "always urged" against predicting "anything that hasn't already happened" [1]. Reversal therefore has to be read as a claim about potential already visible in the present. That makes it hard to state as a forecast later evidence could contradict.

The obsolescence law is the most tractable of the four, because displacement between media is measurable in principle through time-use data. It is also the only one anyone has tried to check, and the check returned uncertainty rather than confirmation [1]. Tyler's account of why is instructive: time-use records are hard to obtain and nearly impossible to reconstruct after the event, multitasking confounds attribution, and causal direction between two media is hard to establish [1]. Each of those is a solvable measurement problem in principle, and none has been solved for the purpose of testing the tetrad.

A final structural obstacle is the closed set of four. Eric McLuhan reports in the introduction to *Laws of Media* that he and his father searched exhaustively for a case requiring a fifth law and found none [3]. A closed set is in principle checkable: a single artefact needing a fifth category would be a disconfirming instance. That is the cheapest test available, and no one appears to have run it in a form that could be published as a result rather than asserted. Proposed fifth laws by later writers — Zingrone's pentad is the standard citation — bear directly on this point, and would convert the closed-set claim into a live question rather than a settled one.

The gap between what a test requires and what the literature contains is therefore not mysterious. The tetrad was built as a probe, defended by analogy when pressed, and used by scholars whose interest was insight rather than prediction [5][1]. Under that description, the absence of tests is a design feature, and the "new science" subtitle is the anomaly that critics have been correcting ever since.


## Open questions

**The Venable exchange has not been read.** The 1976 *Technology and Culture* exchange between William Henry Venable and McLuhan is cited by Tyler as the sustained published critique, and McLuhan's reply is the only place he defends the laws directly against a philosopher-engineer who took the falsifiability claim seriously [1]. Both letters sit behind a paywall. Until they are read, the account here of the retraction rests on later summaries and on the archive's own reframing [5]. The same applies to the report that Levinson treated the Popper framing as not quite literal, which is secondhand [1].

**Harman's chapter has not been read.** "The McLuhans and Metaphysics" (2009) is the most substantial philosophical engagement with the tetrad's status and the basis for extending it to all objects rather than only human artefacts [1]. The chapter was located but not obtained in full, so the object-oriented reading is named here and not assessed.

**Nobody has measured inter-coder reliability.** The failure of two readers to agree on what money obsolesces [3], and the two wine tetrads on one page [1], are anecdotes. No study has taken a set of artefacts, given them to independent analysts with a codebook, and reported agreement statistics. That is the single most useful missing study, and it is cheap.

**The closed-set claim is untested.** Eric McLuhan's report that no case requiring a fifth law was found is an assertion in an introduction, not a published search procedure [3]. Later writers have proposed additional laws — Zingrone's pentad is the standard citation — but those proposals have not been collected and assessed as evidence for or against the closed set.

**The media-displacement literature has moved on.** The studies Tyler marshalled are from 1999 to 2005, before smartphones and streaming [1]. Later work on media substitution and niche competition exists in communication research, and would provide a better evidence base for law two, but it was not reached within this pass. Any claim that the obsolescence quadrant has been tested should be checked against that literature.

**What "application" is worth has not been settled.** The report records that tetrad applications are numerous and untested. It does not establish whether they produce insight that other instruments would miss. That would require comparing tetrad analyses against rival frameworks on the same artefacts, blind, with readers judging which yielded more usable claims — a study nobody appears to have run.

**Coverage was thin on criticism from within media ecology.** Strate, de Kerckhove, Federman and the *Explorations in Media Ecology* literature on the tetrad are named in the outline but were not read in full here. The critical case in this report rests mainly on Tyler, with Eriksen and the *Glocality* essay supplying independent support from outside the McLuhan school [1][4][7]. Three of the ten sources cited here share long passages word for word, suggesting they draw on a common origin or on each other, so they should be counted as fewer independent voices than the citation numbers imply [1][7][9].

## Beyond this question

For anyone using the tetrad as a design or analysis instrument, the findings set a condition rather than a ban. A tetrad that fills four boxes with plausible prose is indistinguishable from one that has been checked, because the instrument supplies no way to tell them apart [1]. The workable discipline is to mark a quadrant empty when the evidence is absent, generate two rival tetrads and report where they disagree, and treat the reversal quadrant as a claim about the present rather than a forecast [1]. Those are exactly the conditions Tyler's own applied tetrad meets, and they are the reason his article is still cited while the applications are not.
